fixes.explanation: Not quite, friend. Hiram, king of Tyre, wasn't David's enemy. The text says “…Hiram had always been a friend of David.” (1 Kings 5:1) So when Hiram sends envoys to Solomon, David's son and Israel's new king, the knock at the door comes from an old friend of the family.

That's it. Solomon, Israel's king, tells Hiram, king of Tyre, “…you know that there are none among us as skilled in logging as the Sidonians.” (1 Kings 5:6) He's saying Hiram's people are the ones for the job.

Yes, baker, and he says it out loud. Hiram, king of Tyre, receives the message from Solomon, Israel's king, and says, “Blessed be the LORD this day! He has given David a wise son over this great people!” (1 Kings 5:7) The text says he rejoiced greatly. The first thing out of his mouth is praise to the LORD.

I think you doubted a good thing here, friend. This one is true. Hiram, king of Tyre, receives Solomon's message and says, “Blessed be the LORD this day! He has given David a wise son over this great people!” (1 Kings 5:7) That's praise for the LORD, and a happy word about David's son.

You've got it, baker. Hiram, king of Tyre, says to Solomon, Israel's king, “And in exchange, you can meet my needs by providing my household with food.” (1 Kings 5:9) So the timber comes with a request: food for his household. Timber on one side, food on the other, and I think both kings walked away happy.

I know some of us can argue over a price tag all day, but that's not in this verse. Hiram, king of Tyre, and Solomon, Israel's king, ended up with this: “There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and the two of them made a treaty.” (1 Kings 5:12) The text says peace, and it says treaty.

Six months would be a long stretch, friend, but that's not the number. Solomon, Israel's king, set it up so the men “…would spend one month in Lebanon and two months at home.” (1 Kings 5:14) The time at home is two months. Then it's back to Lebanon for the next shift.

That's it, baker. The text says the king commanded them “…to quarry large, costly stones to lay the foundation of the temple with dressed stones.” (1 Kings 5:17) That king is Solomon, Israel's king. Dressed stones are stones that have been cut and shaped, so these aren't raw rocks pulled straight from the ground. Large, costly and dressed, all in one order.
